These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: NeuronScope: A Multi-Agent Framework for Explaining Polysemantic Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we faithfully interpret polysemantic neurons in language models by decomposing their activations into atomic semantic components and iteratively refining explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronScope, a multi-agent framework that reformulates neuron interpretation as an iterative, activation-guided process to disentangle polysemantic neurons and produce more faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: NeuronScope is an effective framework for interpreting polysemantic neurons, producing precise, multi-faceted explanations that outperform single-pass baselines.
papers.key_findings:
NeuronScope successfully disentangles hidden polysemanticity in neurons.
NeuronScope produces explanations with higher activation correlation scores compared to single-pass baselines.
The refinement agent consistently improves the score metric across all models and layers.
The decomposition and clustering steps reveal multiple semantic modes in neurons.
The iterative refinement process converges after about five iterations.
papers.limitation:
The iterative, multi-agent refinement process introduces additional computational overhead compared to single-pass interpretation methods, which may limit scalability to very large models or exhaustive neuron-level analysis.
NeuronScope relies on activation-based clustering to identify semantic modes, and its performance may be sensitive to the quality and diversity of the activation samples used.
Evaluation is conducted on natural language text corpora and focuses on neuron behavior under general language usage; extending NeuronScope to more task-specific benchmarks or other modalities remains an open direction.
future_direction: Extending NeuronScope to more task-specific benchmarks or other modalities.
papers.abstract: Neuron-level interpretation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamentally challenged by widespread polysemanticity, where individual neurons respond to multiple distinct semantic concepts. Existing single-pass interpretation methods struggle to faithfully capture such multi-concept behavior. In this work, we propose NeuronScope, a multi-agent framework that reformulates neuron interpretation as an iterative, activation-guided process. NeuronScope explicitly deconstructs neuron activations into atomic semantic components, clusters them into distinct semantic modes, and iteratively refines each explanation using neuron activation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that NeuronScope uncovers hidden polysemanticity and produces explanations with significantly higher activation correlation compared to single-pass baselines.

papers.title: The Strawberry Problem: Emergence of Character-level Understanding in Tokenized Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) consistently fail at simple character-level tasks due to tokenization, and how can this limitation be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a lightweight character-aware architectural modification that significantly improves character-level reasoning in tokenized language models while preserving the inductive advantages of subword tokenization, and analyzes the emergence of this capability through the lens of mutual information and concept percolation.
papers.conclusion: Tokenization creates a bottleneck for character-level understanding in language models, but a lightweight character-aware architecture can mitigate this issue, and the emergence of this capability follows a percolation model similar to concept learning.
papers.key_findings:
Character-level understanding emerges late in training and is dependent on vocabulary size and the number of characters per token.
The proposed character-aware module eliminates the dependence on vocabulary size, leading to earlier and more stable emergence of character-level capabilities.
The emergence dynamics for character-level understanding align with predictions from concept percolation models, suggesting it is similar to learning concept-property associations.
The character-aware architecture improves performance on character-level tasks even when trained on real-world data with pretrained tokenizers (GPT-2, LLaMA-2).
The character encoder can be significantly downsized without major performance loss, and placing the cross-attention in the middle of the main model yields the best results.
papers.limitation: The experiments were conducted in a synthetic and idealized setup to understand the phenomena without confounding factors; the impact on real-world scenarios needs validation at larger scales.
papers.abstract: Despite their remarkable progress across diverse domains, Large Language Models (LLMs) consistently fail at simple character-level tasks, such as counting letters in words, due to a fundamental limitation: tokenization. In this work, we frame this limitation as a problem of low mutual information and analyze it in terms of concept emergence. Using a suite of 19 synthetic tasks that isolate character-level reasoning in a controlled setting, we show that such capabilities emerge suddenly and only late in training. We find that percolation-based models of concept emergence explain these patterns, suggesting that learning character composition is not fundamentally different from learning commonsense knowledge. To address this bottleneck, we propose a lightweight architectural modification that significantly improves character-level reasoning while preserving the inductive advantages of subword models. Together, our results bridge low-level perceptual gaps in tokenized LMs and provide a principled framework for understanding and mitigating their structural blind spots. We make our code publicly available.

papers.title: Extending Machine Language Models toward Human-Level Language Understanding
papers.research_question: How can machine language models be extended toward human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems, inspired by cognitive neuroscience?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a brain and AI-inspired framework for language understanding that integrates language with other modalities and memory systems to overcome limitations of current language models, which focus exclusively on language-internal tasks and lack memory for prior situations.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will lead to better language understanding systems that approach human-level capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models focus on language-internal tasks and lack understanding of situations.
They lack memory for prior situations outside a fixed contextual span.
The brain's understanding system integrates language with other modalities and has a fast-learning memory system (medial temporal lobe).
Future models should incorporate multi-modal inputs and an MTL-like memory to achieve human-level understanding.
Situated agents in interactive environments can enhance compositionality and data efficiency.
future_direction: Incorporating multi-modal inputs (visual, auditory, etc.) and an MTL-like memory system.
Extending the framework to abstract situations beyond concrete, here-and-now situations.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem for control and task guidance.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. The human ability to understand and communicate about situations emerges gradually from experience and depends on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on \emph{query-based attention}, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: Emergence of Phonemic, Syntactic, and Semantic Representations in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Whether and when phonemic, lexical and syntactic representations emerge in the activations of artificial neural networks during their training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that speech- and text-based models follow a sequence of learning stages where phonemic, lexical, and syntactic representations emerge in their activations, but require 2 to 4 orders of magnitude more data than children for these representations to emerge.
papers.conclusion: These results show conditions under which major stages of language acquisition spontaneously emerge in neural networks, delineating a promising path to understand the computations underpinning language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Phonemic structure, mirroring articulatory features, emerges in self-supervised speech models.
Lexical semantic structure (WordNet hypernymy) emerges in both text and speech models, but more strongly in text models.
Syntactic structure (dependency trees) emerges in both text and speech models.
The order of acquisition in audio models is phonemic, then partial lexical semantic, then syntactic.
Models require 2-4 orders of magnitude more data than children for these linguistic representations to emerge.
papers.limitation:
The models require 2 to 4 orders of magnitude more data than children for linguistic representations to emerge.
The semantic code only partially emerges in audio models, with scores potentially explained by acoustic correlates.
papers.abstract: During language acquisition, children successively learn to categorize phonemes, identify words, and combine them with syntax to form new meaning. While the development of this behavior is well characterized, we still lack a unifying computational framework to explain its underlying neural representations. Here, we investigate whether and when phonemic, lexical, and syntactic representations emerge in the activations of artificial neural networks during their training. Our results show that both speech- and text-based models follow a sequence of learning stages: during training, their neural activations successively build subspaces, where the geometry of the neural activations represents phonemic, lexical, and syntactic structure. While this developmental trajectory qualitatively relates to children's, it is quantitatively different: These algorithms indeed require two to four orders of magnitude more data for these neural representations to emerge. Together, these results show conditions under which major stages of language acquisition spontaneously emerge, and hence delineate a promising path to understand the computations underpinning language acquisition.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: Partner Modelling Emerges in Recurrent Agents (But Only When It Matters)
papers.research_question: Does partner modeling require explicit, dedicated mechanisms, or can it emerge spontaneously from the pressures of open-ended cooperative interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Partner modeling can arise spontaneously in simple model-free RNN agents solely from the demands of flexible cooperation, without explicit incentives or specialized architectures, but only under environmental conditions that impose social pressure (i.e., when agents can influence partner behavior).
papers.conclusion: Social intelligence, in the form of partner modeling, can emerge from specific environmental pressures acting in concert with general learning and memory mechanisms, rather than necessarily relying on unique architectures.
papers.key_findings:
RNN agents trained with diverse partners outperform MLP and single-partner RNN baselines, indicating emergent partner modeling that generalizes to unseen collaborators.
Hidden states of the RNN encode partner task abilities (as shown by linear probe accuracy and UMAP structure) when the agent has the ability to influence task allocation.
Agents can adapt online to new partners within a single episode, recovering performance after a mid-episode partner switch.
Partner modeling emerges even in 'blind' agents trained without visual input, relying solely on egocentric signals and task reward.
The emergence of structured partner representations is significantly weakened when agents are denied the ability to influence partner behavior.
papers.limitation:
Experiments used only a single cooperative environment (Overcooked-AI), though preliminary tests were done in CoinGame.
The study focused on relatively simple forms of representation, not complex hierarchical representations like how others perceive the agent in turn.
The implementation of 'influence' was strong (direct control), unlike the more nuanced ways humans influence collaborators.
future_direction: Generalize findings to other environments, especially open-ended ones, and scale to more than one teammate.
Investigate transformer-based agents and whether attention mechanisms implicitly track partner strategies.
Explore transferring internal partner representations between agents and tasks via hidden state initialization.
papers.abstract: Humans are remarkably adept at collaboration, able to infer the strengths and weaknesses of new partners in order to work successfully towards shared goals. To build AI systems with this capability, we must first understand its building blocks: does such flexibility require explicit, dedicated mechanisms for modelling others -- or can it emerge spontaneously from the pressures of open-ended cooperative interaction? To investigate this question, we train simple model-free RNN agents to collaborate with a population of diverse partners. Using the `Overcooked-AI' environment, we collect data from thousands of collaborative teams, and analyse agents' internal hidden states. Despite a lack of additional architectural features, inductive biases, or auxiliary objectives, the agents nevertheless develop structured internal representations of their partners' task abilities, enabling rapid adaptation and generalisation to novel collaborators. We investigated these internal models through probing techniques, and large-scale behavioural analysis. Notably, we find that structured partner modelling emerges when agents can influence partner behaviour by controlling task allocation. Our results show that partner modelling can arise spontaneously in model-free agents -- but only under environmental conditions that impose the right kind of social pressure.

papers.title: Why are LLMs' abilities emergent?
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models exhibit emergent abilities, and what are the underlying principles of this emergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that emergent abilities in LLMs arise from the complex nonlinear dynamics of deep neural networks, similar to emergent phenomena in other complex systems like physics and biology.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the capabilities acquired by DNNs are emergent properties arising from the cooperative dynamics of simple components, requiring a recognition of DNNs as complex dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent abilities in LLMs are not solely due to parameter scaling but result from complex dynamics of nonlinear systems.
Grokking phenomena show that models can suddenly generalize after periods of overfitting, indicating delayed emergence.
Phase transitions and sudden improvements in model capabilities are analogous to emergent behaviors in other domains.
DNNs exhibit high sensitivity to initial conditions and small changes, contributing to emergent properties.
Current definitions of emergence in LLMs are too phenomenological and should focus on internal dynamic transformations.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in generative tasks has raised fundamental questions about the nature of their acquired capabilities, which often appear to emerge unexpectedly without explicit training. This paper examines the emergent properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) through both theoretical analysis and empirical observation, addressing the epistemological challenge of "creation without understanding" that characterises contemporary AI development. We explore how the neural approach's reliance on nonlinear, stochastic processes fundamentally differs from symbolic computational paradigms, creating systems whose macro-level behaviours cannot be analytically derived from micro-level neuron activities. Through analysis of scaling laws, grokking phenomena, and phase transitions in model capabilities, I demonstrate that emergent abilities arise from the complex dynamics of highly sensitive nonlinear systems rather than simply from parameter scaling alone. My investigation reveals that current debates over metrics, pre-training loss thresholds, and in-context learning miss the fundamental ontological nature of emergence in DNNs. I argue that these systems exhibit genuine emergent properties analogous to those found in other complex natural phenomena, where systemic capabilities emerge from cooperative interactions among simple components without being reducible to their individual behaviours. The paper concludes that understanding LLM capabilities requires recognising DNNs as a new domain of complex dynamical systems governed by universal principles of emergence, similar to those operating in physics, chemistry, and biology. This perspective shifts the focus from purely phenomenological definitions of emergence to understanding the internal dynamic transformations that enable these systems to acquire capabilities that transcend their individual components.

papers.title: Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis of Neuron Interaction Dynamics in Large Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantitatively analyze the internal structures and mechanisms driving emergent abilities in large models, moving beyond traditional observation-based methods that focus on model size and output performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis (NeuroMFA), a framework for structural analysis of large models, and proposes a novel structure-based metric to quantify the degree of emergence by analyzing neuron interaction dynamics during training.
papers.conclusion: NeuroMFA provides a quantitative framework for analyzing emergent abilities in large models by linking structural self-organization to capability development, offering a new perspective beyond traditional observation-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed degree of emergence metric correlates with model performance on standard benchmarks, indicating its validity as a proxy for emergent abilities.
Larger models exhibit more pronounced self-organization and structural emergence during training, as captured by the NeuroMFA metrics.
The method can differentiate between model architectures, showing that transformer-based models exhibit clearer multifractal structure and self-organization compared to CNNs.
The critical point for emergence occurs at similar training steps across models trained on different datasets, but the rate of increase in emergence can vary with data quality.
The framework provides a quantitative link between the internal structural dynamics of a model and the development of its capabilities.
papers.limitation: The framework demonstrates correlations between the emergence metric and downstream performance but has not yet established a clear causal relationship.
future_direction: Future work should focus on identifying specific linguistic phenomena captured by LLMs and demonstrating how the analysis methods can reveal the learning process of these phenomena during training, thereby establishing a stronger causal connection.
Further research is needed to apply the framework to a wider range of model architectures and tasks.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been increasing attention on the capabilities of large models, particularly in handling complex tasks that small-scale models are unable to perform. Notably, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated ``intelligent'' abilities such as complex reasoning and abstract language comprehension, reflecting cognitive-like behaviors. However, current research on emergent abilities in large models predominantly focuses on the relationship between model performance and size, leaving a significant gap in the systematic quantitative analysis of the internal structures and mechanisms driving these emergent abilities. Drawing inspiration from neuroscience research on brain network structure and self-organization, we propose (i) a general network representation of large models, (ii) a new analytical framework, called Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis (NeuroMFA), for structural analysis, and (iii) a novel structure-based metric as a proxy for emergent abilities of large models. By linking structural features to the capabilities of large models, NeuroMFA provides a quantitative framework for analyzing emergent phenomena in large models. Our experiments show that the proposed method yields a comprehensive measure of network's evolving heterogeneity and organization, offering theoretical foundations and a new perspective for investigating emergent abilities in large models.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: A Philosophical Introduction to Language Models - Part II: The Way Forward
papers.research_question: What are the philosophical implications of recent progress in LLMs, particularly regarding interpretability, multimodality, consciousness, reproducibility, and their relevance to modeling human cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a philosophical exploration of issues raised by LLMs, arguing for the importance of mechanistic interpretability through causal intervention methods and discussing the implications of multimodal extensions, consciousness debates, and reproducibility concerns.
papers.conclusion: LLM-like systems may be relevant to modeling aspects of human cognition if their architectural characteristics and learning scenarios are adequately constrained, but further research is needed to address interpretability and reproducibility challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Benchmarks for LLMs are limited by saturation, gamification, contamination, and construct validity issues, which undermine their reliability for assessing model capacities.
Causal intervention methods, such as ablation and activation editing, are necessary for achieving mechanistic understanding of LLMs' internal representations and computations.
Multimodal models often exhibit compositional failures due to their training objectives (e.g., contrastive learning) rather than inherent architectural limitations of the Transformer.
There are ongoing debates about whether LLMs could meet minimal criteria for consciousness, though current evidence is insufficient and the analogy to biological consciousness is problematic.
LLM research faces significant issues of secrecy and reproducibility, which hinder scientific progress and trust in reported capabilities.
future_direction: Advancing mechanistic interpretability through causal intervention methods to understand LLMs' internal mechanisms.
Addressing reproducibility and secrecy issues in LLM research to foster open scientific inquiry.
Exploring the potential of LLMs as models of human cognition by constraining their architecture and learning scenarios appropriately.
papers.abstract: In this paper, the second of two companion pieces, we explore novel philosophical questions raised by recent progress in large language models (LLMs) that go beyond the classical debates covered in the first part. We focus particularly on issues related to interpretability, examining evidence from causal intervention methods about the nature of LLMs' internal representations and computations. We also discuss the implications of multimodal and modular extensions of LLMs, recent debates about whether such systems may meet minimal criteria for consciousness, and concerns about secrecy and reproducibility in LLM research. Finally, we discuss whether LLM-like systems may be relevant to modeling aspects of human cognition, if their architectural characteristics and learning scenario are adequately constrained.

papers.title: Compositional Generalization in Grounded Language Learning via Induced Model Sparsity
papers.research_question: How can induced model sparsity help achieve compositional generalization and sample efficiency in grounded language learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Sparse Factored Attention model that leverages sparsity and factor compositionality to achieve compositional generalization and sample efficiency in grounded language learning for navigation tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that induced sparsity and factor compositionality enable compositional generalization and sample efficiency in grounded language learning, as demonstrated by the Sparse Factored Attention model.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Factored Attention achieves high performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution goals with few samples.
The model learns correct correspondences between words and attributes, as shown by visualization of embedding correlations.
Standard architectures (Transformer, FiLM) fail to generalize compositionally or require large amounts of data.
The proposed training method with a discriminator enables learning goal identification without labels.
The decoupled architecture (goal identification + planning) improves sample efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The goal identification and planning methods do not work over compound goals.
The discriminator training method requires that the dataset can be partitioned into subsets corresponding to each goal.
Measuring sample efficiency is not well-specified because each training step could improve the model arbitrarily.
The environment assumptions are strong: fully observable state space, knowledge of connectivity, and disentangled factors.
papers.abstract: We provide a study of how induced model sparsity can help achieve compositional generalization and better sample efficiency in grounded language learning problems. We consider simple language-conditioned navigation problems in a grid world environment with disentangled observations. We show that standard neural architectures do not always yield compositional generalization. To address this, we design an agent that contains a goal identification module that encourages sparse correlations between words in the instruction and attributes of objects, composing them together to find the goal. The output of the goal identification module is the input to a value iteration network planner. Our agent maintains a high level of performance on goals containing novel combinations of properties even when learning from a handful of demonstrations. We examine the internal representations of our agent and find the correct correspondences between words in its dictionary and attributes in the environment.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Lost in Translation: The Algorithmic Gap Between LMs and the Brain
papers.research_question: What is the algorithmic gap between language models and the human brain, and how can we bridge it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that despite computational-level equivalence in some tasks, language models diverge from human cognition at the algorithmic level, and proposes neuroscience-inspired architectural and training changes to bridge this gap.
papers.conclusion: The intelligence emerging from current LMs is fundamentally different from human cognition, and incorporating brain-inspired constraints may lead to AI with human-like flexibility and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language models and the brain show representational similarities but likely use different algorithms.
Current LMs lack brain-like features such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning.
Incorporating brain-inspired features could lead to more human-like AI and better models of cognition.
future_direction: Incorporate sparse connectivity and modularity (e.g., MoE, RIMs) in LMs.
Add internal states and recurrence to transformers.
Develop continual and curriculum learning methods for LMs.
Ground LMs in embodied and social interactions.
Integrate oscillatory dynamics and scaling laws with efficiency constraints.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) have achieved impressive performance on various linguistic tasks, but their relationship to human language processing in the brain remains unclear. This paper examines the gaps and overlaps between LMs and the brain at different levels of analysis, emphasizing the importance of looking beyond input-output behavior to examine and compare the internal processes of these systems. We discuss how insights from neuroscience, such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning, can inform the development of more biologically plausible language models. Furthermore, we explore the role of scaling laws in bridging the gap between LMs and human cognition, highlighting the need for efficiency constraints analogous to those in biological systems. By developing LMs that more closely mimic brain function, we aim to advance both artificial intelligence and our understanding of human cognition.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Emergence of symbolic abstraction heads for in-context learning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do small transformer models recognize, learn, and generalize abstract sequential symbolic patterns, and do they form internal symbolic representations through abstraction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Small transformer models can learn abstract symbolic patterns and develop abstraction heads for in-context learning, enabling symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Small transformer models can recognize and generalize abstract patterns through abstraction heads, providing insights for neuro-symbolic processing.
papers.key_findings:
Models with 2 or 3 layers successfully solve abstract pattern matching tasks, while 1-layer models fail.
Abstraction heads emerge in attention mechanisms, attending to the first instantiation to generalize patterns.
Variable matching is a simpler task that can be solved even by single-layer models without abstraction.
Training loss shows bumps that correlate with sudden improvements in accuracy, indicating learning of critical strategies.
Abstraction heads operate at a more abstract level than induction heads, focusing on pattern matching from instantiations.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are based on simplified sequences of numbers and may not generalize to human language or complex relations.
The study is limited to small transformer models with 1-3 layers, and different mechanisms may emerge in larger models.
future_direction: Investigate alternative mechanisms for abstract pattern matching in transformers.
Explore the emergence of abstraction heads in larger models with more layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on self-attention circuits are able to perform, at inference time, novel reasoning tasks, but the mechanisms inside the models are currently not fully understood. We assume that LLMs are able to generalize abstract patterns from the input and form an internal symbolic internal representation of the content. In this paper, we study this by analyzing the performance of small LLM models trained with sequences of instantiations of abstract sequential symbolic patterns or templates. It is shown that even a model with two layers is able to learn an abstract template and use it to generate correct output representing the pattern. This can be seen as a form of symbolic inference taking place inside the network. In this paper, we call the emergent mechanism abstraction head. Identifying mechanisms of symbolic reasoning in a neural network can help to find new ways to merge symbolic and neural processing.

papers.title: Measuring Compositionality in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we measure compositional structure in learned representations? And how does compositionality relate to learning dynamics, human judgments, representational similarity, and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Tree Reconstruction Error (TRE), a method for measuring compositional structure in learned representations, and applies it to study compositionality in relation to learning dynamics, human judgments, similarity, and generalization.
papers.conclusion: TRE provides a tool for evaluating compositionality in representation learning, opening up new directions for understanding models and the conditions that give rise to compositional representations.
papers.key_findings:
TRE tracks compositionality over learning, showing compression in the information bottleneck framework is associated with discovery of compositional representations.
TRE correlates with human judgments of compositionality for noun-noun compounds.
Compositionality (low TRE) imposes constraints on similarity between representations (Proposition 1).
In communication games, compositionality is correlated with generalization error, but low TRE is not necessary for good generalization and can sometimes indicate trivial strategies.
papers.limitation:
TRE requires oracle derivations (known compositional structure of inputs)
Low TRE can correspond to trivial strategies that yield poor overall performance
future_direction: Generalizing TRE to settings without oracle derivations (unsupervised grammar induction)
Using TRE to better understand existing machine learning models
Understanding data distributions and loss functions that give rise to compositional representations
papers.abstract: Many machine learning algorithms represent input data with vector embeddings or discrete codes. When inputs exhibit compositional structure (e.g. objects built from parts or procedures from subroutines), it is natural to ask whether this compositional structure is reflected in the the inputs' learned representations. While the assessment of compositionality in languages has received significant attention in linguistics and adjacent fields, the machine learning literature lacks general-purpose tools for producing graded measurements of compositional structure in more general (e.g. vector-valued) representation spaces. We describe a procedure for evaluating compositionality by measuring how well the true representation-producing model can be approximated by a model that explicitly composes a collection of inferred representational primitives. We use the procedure to provide formal and empirical characterizations of compositional structure in a variety of settings, exploring the relationship between compositionality and learning dynamics, human judgments, representational similarity, and generalization.

papers.title: LoFiT: Localized Fine-tuning on LLM Representations
papers.research_question: Can localized fine-tuning serve as an effective alternative to representation intervention methods for adapting LLMs? Can representation offsets be more effectively obtained via learning than via representation intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LOFIT, a localized fine-tuning method that modifies representations of a small number of attention heads, achieving competitive performance with far fewer parameters than other PEFT methods.
papers.conclusion: LOFIT demonstrates that localized fine-tuning is an effective alternative to representation intervention, and that interpretability insights can be combined with PEFT for strong performance with minimal parameters.
papers.key_findings:
LOFIT outperforms representation intervention methods like ITI and RepE on truthfulness and reasoning tasks.
Localization is important: using task-specific attention heads leads to better performance than using heads from other tasks.
LOFIT achieves comparable performance to other PEFT methods like LoRA, RED, and ReFT while modifying 20x-200x fewer parameters.
LOFIT shows better generalizability to out-of-domain settings compared to other PEFT methods.
The attention heads selected by LOFIT are task-specific and not interchangeable across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments focus on English-language truthfulness and reasoning datasets with short contexts and responses; different behaviors might occur for long-context or long-form generation tasks.
Only evaluated autoregressive Transformer language models up to 13B parameters; different behavior could be observed at larger scales.
papers.abstract: Recent work in interpretability shows that large language models (LLMs) can be adapted for new tasks in a learning-free way: it is possible to intervene on LLM representations to elicit desired behaviors for alignment. For instance, adding certain bias vectors to the outputs of certain attention heads is reported to boost the truthfulness of models. In this work, we show that localized fine-tuning serves as an effective alternative to such representation intervention methods. We introduce a framework called Localized Fine-Tuning on LLM Representations (LoFiT), which identifies a subset of attention heads that are most important for learning a specific task, then trains offset vectors to add to the model's hidden representations at those selected heads. LoFiT localizes to a sparse set of heads (3%-10%) and learns the offset vectors from limited training data, comparable to the settings used for representation intervention. For truthfulness and reasoning tasks, we find that LoFiT's intervention vectors are more effective for LLM adaptation than vectors from representation intervention methods such as Inference-time Intervention. We also find that the localization step is important: selecting a task-specific set of attention heads can lead to higher performance than intervening on heads selected for a different task. Finally, across 7 tasks we study, LoFiT achieves comparable performance to other parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA, despite modifying 20x-200x fewer parameters than these methods.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: A Percolation Model of Emergence: Analyzing Transformers Trained on a Formal Language
papers.research_question: What is a phenomenological definition of emergence in neural networks, and can it be observed and explained in a controlled experimental system using Transformers trained on a formal language?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a phenomenological definition of emergence in neural networks, demonstrates emergent capabilities in Transformers trained on a formal language, and introduces a percolation model that predicts the scaling of emergence.
papers.conclusion: The experimental and theoretical frameworks yield a step towards better defining, characterizing, and predicting emergence in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on a context-sensitive formal language exhibit emergent capabilities, with sudden performance improvements on multiple tasks.
The sudden improvements correlate with the model learning the underlying grammatical rules and type constraints of the language.
A percolation model based on bipartite graph theory predicts the scaling of the emergence point with changes in data structure.
The transition point for emergence scales as a power law in the number of properties in the language.
The study provides an experimental system to study emergence in a controlled setting.
papers.abstract: Increase in data, size, or compute can lead to sudden learning of specific capabilities by a neural network -- a phenomenon often called "emergence''. Beyond scientific understanding, establishing the causal factors underlying such emergent capabilities is crucial to enable risk regulation frameworks for AI. In this work, we seek inspiration from study of emergent properties in other fields and propose a phenomenological definition for the concept in the context of neural networks. Our definition implicates the acquisition of general structures underlying the data-generating process as a cause of sudden performance growth for specific, narrower tasks. We empirically investigate this definition by proposing an experimental system grounded in a context-sensitive formal language and find that Transformers trained to perform tasks on top of strings from this language indeed exhibit emergent capabilities. Specifically, we show that once the language's underlying grammar and context-sensitivity inducing structures are learned by the model, performance on narrower tasks suddenly begins to improve. We then analogize our network's learning dynamics with the process of percolation on a bipartite graph, establishing a formal phase transition model that predicts the shift in the point of emergence observed in our experiments when changing the data structure. Overall, our experimental and theoretical frameworks yield a step towards better defining, characterizing, and predicting emergence in neural networks.

papers.title: Meaning without reference in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models achieve meaning through conceptual role theory, even without direct reference to the real world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve meaning through conceptual role theory, where meaning is derived from the relationships between internal representational states, rather than requiring reference to the real world.
papers.conclusion: LLMs likely already share the foundation of how human concepts get their meaning through conceptual role theory.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs likely capture important aspects of meaning through conceptual role, approximating human cognition.
Meaning arises from the interrelations between concepts, which LLMs can learn from text prediction.
Reference is not necessary for meaning; many meaningful concepts lack referents.
LLMs' internal geometries and trajectories approximate those of humans, supporting conceptual role theory.
Text provides clues to conceptual role because human conceptual roles generated the text.
papers.limitation: LLMs do not perfectly capture human concepts and lack aspects like reference, inference, better compositionality, and consistent abstract reasoning.
future_direction: Enrich the internal conceptual roles of LLMs to better reflect human structure, inference, and algorithmic sophistication.
Incorporate multimodal data and experience to improve meaning.
papers.abstract: The widespread success of large language models (LLMs) has been met with skepticism that they possess anything like human concepts or meanings. Contrary to claims that LLMs possess no meaning whatsoever, we argue that they likely capture important aspects of meaning, and moreover work in a way that approximates a compelling account of human cognition in which meaning arises from conceptual role. Because conceptual role is defined by the relationships between internal representational states, meaning cannot be determined from a model's architecture, training data, or objective function, but only by examination of how its internal states relate to each other. This approach may clarify why and how LLMs are so successful and suggest how they can be made more human-like.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Does Representation Matter? Exploring Intermediate Layers in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What defines a 'good' representation in large language models, and how does the quality of intermediate representations compare to final layers across different architectures and settings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that intermediate layers of LLMs often provide better representations for downstream tasks than final layers, and reveals significant differences in representation quality and evolution between Transformer and State Space Model (SSM) architectures.
papers.conclusion: The research advances understanding of internal representation dynamics in LLMs, highlighting the pivotal role of intermediate layers and the distinct behaviors of Transformer and SSM architectures, providing guidance for model optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers on downstream embedding tasks from the MTEB benchmark.
Prompt entropy in intermediate layers is negatively correlated with MMLU performance for Transformers like Llama3, but not for SSMs like Mamba2.
Transformers exhibit greater representational variability and information compression in intermediate layers, while SSMs show more stable representations across layers.
Training effects on representation quality are most pronounced in intermediate layers, with prompt entropy decreasing and InfoNCE peaking as training progresses.
Extreme input conditions (token repetition, randomness, and length) distinctly affect prompt entropy, particularly in intermediate layers, and a bimodal entropy distribution is observed in Transformer intermediate layers with an unknown cause.
papers.limitation: The cause of the bimodal entropy distribution observed in intermediate layers of Transformer models remains unknown.
future_direction: Investigate the causes of bimodal entropy distributions in intermediate layers.
Explore the development of new metrics specifically tailored to LLMs for representation evaluation.
papers.abstract: Understanding what defines a good representation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamental to both theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this paper, we investigate the quality of intermediate representations in various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs). We find that intermediate layers often yield more informative representations for downstream tasks than the final layers. To measure the representation quality, we adapt and apply a suite of metrics - such as prompt entropy, curvature, and augmentation-invariance - originally proposed in other contexts. Our empirical study reveals significant architectural differences, how representations evolve throughout training, and how factors like input randomness and prompt length affect each layer. Notably, we observe a bimodal pattern in the entropy of some intermediate layers and consider potential explanations tied to training data. Overall, our results illuminate the internal mechanics of LLMs and guide strategies for architectural optimization and training.

papers.title: A Compositional Neural Architecture for Language
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical structure and compositionality in language be reconciled with principles from cell assembly computation in neuroscience?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a neural architecture based on multidimensional coordinate systems and gain modulation to explain how the brain achieves compositional and hierarchical language processing.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a neural architecture that unifies insights from linguistics, psycholinguistics, and neuroscience to explain how the brain achieves compositional language processing through gain modulation and neural oscillations.
papers.key_findings:
The neural architecture uses a manifold of neural trajectories to encode sensory, motor, and abstract linguistic states.
Gain modulation, including inhibition, tunes the path in the manifold and infers latent structure.
Predictive information about upcoming sensory input during production and comprehension is available without a separate operation.
The architecture synthesizes neural entrainment to speech, systems neuroscience, category theory, and a symbolic-connectionist computational model (DORA) that uses time and rhythm.
The proposal moves toward unifying insights from linguistics and psycholinguistics with neural computation.
papers.abstract: Hierarchical structure and compositionality imbue human language with unparalleled expressive power and set it apart from other perception-action systems. However, neither formal nor neurobiological models account for how these defining computational properties might arise in a physiological system. I attempt to reconcile hierarchy and compositionality with principles from cell assembly computation in neuroscience; the result is an emerging theory of how the brain could convert distributed perceptual representations into hierarchical structures across multiple timescales while representing interpretable incremental stages of (de)compositional meaning. The model's architecture-a multidimensional coordinate system based on neurophysiological models of sensory processing-proposes that a manifold of neural trajectories encodes sensory, motor, and abstract linguistic states. Gain modulation, including inhibition, tunes the path in the manifold in accordance with behavior and is how latent structure is inferred. As a consequence, predictive information about upcoming sensory input during production and comprehension is available without a separate operation. The proposed processing mechanism is synthesized from current models of neural entrainment to speech, concepts from systems neuroscience and category theory, and a symbolic-connectionist computational model that uses time and rhythm to structure information. I build on evidence from cognitive neuroscience and computational modeling that suggests a formal and mechanistic alignment between structure building and neural oscillations, and moves toward unifying basic insights from linguistics and psycholinguistics with the currency of neural computation.

papers.title: Hedonic Neurons: A Mechanistic Mapping of Latent Coalitions in Transformer MLPs
papers.research_question: How do neurons in transformer MLPs cooperate to encode task-specific features after fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a game-theoretic framework to discover and analyze stable coalitions of neurons in transformer MLPs, revealing how they cooperate to encode task-specific features.
papers.conclusion: HedonicNeurons provides a principled foundation for uncovering how cooperative computational units emerge, evolve, and specialize in large-scale language models.
papers.key_findings:
Hedonic coalitions achieve consistently higher synergy than clustering baselines.
Ablation of hedonic coalitions yields 3–5× larger out-of-distribution performance drops, indicating functional importance.
Coalition activations align strongly with IR heuristics, with R2 improvements from ~0.15 to 0.55–0.67.
Coalitions used as macro-features improve predictive R2 from ~0.20 to 0.43–0.47 on OOD sets.
Tracking coalitions across layers shows that most groups vanish or split, suggesting MLPs act as feature filters.
papers.limitation: Utilities depend on layer-local logits and second-order ablations, omitting higher-order interactions and attention mechanisms.
future_direction: Extend to overlapping coalitions via fractional hedonic games.
Integrate attention heads for joint sub-module analysis.
Design low-variance estimators to reduce O(n^2) ablation costs.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich task-specific features, but the form of these representations, especially within MLP layers, remains unclear. Empirical inspection of LoRA updates shows that new features concentrate in mid-layer MLPs, yet the scale of these layers obscures meaningful structure. Prior probing suggests that statistical priors may strengthen, split, or vanish across depth, motivating the need to study how neurons work together rather than in isolation. We introduce a mechanistic interpretability framework based on coalitional game theory, where neurons mimic agents in a hedonic game whose preferences capture their synergistic contributions to layer-local computations. Using top-responsive utilities and the PAC-Top-Cover algorithm, we extract stable coalitions of neurons: groups whose joint ablation has non-additive effects. We then track their transitions across layers as persistence, splitting, merging, or disappearance. Applied to LLaMA, Mistral, and Pythia rerankers fine-tuned on scalar IR tasks, our method finds coalitions with consistently higher synergy than clustering baselines. By revealing how neurons cooperate to encode features, hedonic coalitions uncover higher-order structure beyond disentanglement and yield computational units that are functionally important, interpretable, and predictive across domains.

papers.title: Emergence of a High-Dimensional Abstraction Phase in Language Transformers
papers.research_question: What does the evolution of intrinsic dimension (ID) over layers reveal about representational generalizability and linguistic processing in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a distinct high-dimensionality phase in the intermediate layers of language transformers, which corresponds to the first full linguistic abstraction of the input and is predictive of model performance.
papers.conclusion: Different LMs consistently develop a central-layer phase where the intrinsic dimension is expanded, which is the locus of deeper linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
A distinct phase characterized by a peak in the intrinsic dimension of representations emerges in intermediate layers across five transformer-based LMs.
This high-ID phase is significantly reduced with random text and absent in untrained models, indicating it reflects learned linguistic structure.
The layer at which the ID peak appears correlates with language modeling quality.
The highest-dimensional representations of different networks predict each other, suggesting they encode similar abstract information.
The ID peak marks a transition from surface-form to syntactic and semantic processing, and representations within it are the first to viably transfer to downstream tasks.
papers.limitation: The paper focuses on detecting broad qualitative patterns; future work should establish a clearer causal connection between intrinsic dimension and language processing via layer ablation studies.
future_direction: Establish causal connection via layer ablations and constraining dimensionality during processing.
Test the effect of pruning inside and outside the ID peak.
Study the relation between the ID profile and specific circuits detected in mechanistic interpretability work.
Use ID profiles for model pruning, fine-tuning, model stitching, and brain encoding models.
papers.abstract: A language model (LM) is a mapping from a linguistic context to an output token. However, much remains to be known about this mapping, including how its geometric properties relate to its function. We take a high-level geometric approach to its analysis, observing, across five pre-trained transformer-based LMs and three input datasets, a distinct phase characterized by high intrinsic dimensionality. During this phase, representations (1) correspond to the first full linguistic abstraction of the input; (2) are the first to viably transfer to downstream tasks; (3) predict each other across different LMs. Moreover, we find that an earlier onset of the phase strongly predicts better language modelling performance. In short, our results suggest that a central high-dimensionality phase underlies core linguistic processing in many common LM architectures.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
