However, little effort has been spent on improving RNN architectures and on understanding the underlying neural mechanisms for performance gain. In this paper, we propose a novel, multiple-timescale, stochastic RNN for RL. Empirical results show that the network can autonomously learn to abstract sub-goals and can self-develop an action hierarchy using internal dynamics in a challenging continuous control task. Furthermore, we show that the self-developed compositionality of the network enhances faster re-learning when adapting to a new task that is a re-composition of previously learned sub-goals, than when starting from scratch. We also found that improved performance can be achieved when neural activities are subject to stochastic rather than deterministic dynamics.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: A Brain-like Synergistic Core in LLMs Drives Behaviour and Learning
papers.research_question: Does the synergistic information processing core, similar to that in the human brain, emerge in LLMs through learning, and is it functionally critical for behavior and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs spontaneously develop a synergistic information processing core in their middle layers, similar to the human brain, which is causally important for model performance and enhances generalization during reinforcement learning fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit a synergistic core in middle layers and a redundant periphery, mirroring the human brain, and this core can be causally manipulated to impair or enhance performance, validating synergy as a key metric for understanding generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs exhibit synergistic interactions, while early and late layers are redundant.
This synergistic core emerges through training and is absent in randomly initialized networks.
Ablating synergistic components causes disproportionate performance degradation.
Fine-tuning synergistic cores with reinforcement learning yields greater performance improvements than fine-tuning redundant components.
The synergistic core has high global efficiency, matching topological properties of the human brain.
papers.limitation:
Focus on attention heads and Mixture-of-Experts modules, not Multilayer Perceptrons.
Reliance on L2 norm of attention outputs as a proxy for activation, which is a simplification.
Computational constraints limited experiments to fine-tuning rather than full-scale pretraining.
Use of custom cognitive task categories instead of standard, large-scale benchmarks.
future_direction: Apply information decomposition techniques to MLP layers.
Use more refined metrics that account for the vector-space geometry of representations.
Validate whether targeted synergistic updates can accelerate initial model convergence during pretraining.
papers.abstract: The independent evolution of intelligence in biological and artificial systems offers a unique opportunity to identify its fundamental computational principles. Here we show that large language models spontaneously develop synergistic cores -- components where information integration exceeds individual parts -- remarkably similar to those in the human brain. Using principles of information decomposition across multiple LLM model families and architectures, we find that areas in middle layers exhibit synergistic processing while early and late layers rely on redundancy, mirroring the informational organisation in biological brains. This organisation emerges through learning and is absent in randomly initialised networks. Crucially, ablating synergistic components causes disproportionate behavioural changes and performance loss, aligning with theoretical predictions about the fragility of synergy. Moreover, fine-tuning synergistic regions through reinforcement learning yields significantly greater performance gains than training redundant components, yet supervised fine-tuning shows no such advantage. This convergence suggests that synergistic information processing is a fundamental property of intelligence, providing targets for principled model design and testable predictions for biological intelligence.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: Analyzing Transformer Dynamics as Movement through Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do the underlying mechanics of Transformer-based language models give rise to intelligent behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space, establishing a 'Theory of Transformers' where intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the model's composition functions.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a unified framework for understanding Transformers as movement through embedding space, explaining how intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the dynamics of encoding and decoding walks.
papers.key_findings:
Intelligent behaviors map to paths in Embedding Space which the Transformer random-walks through during inference.
LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths, assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors.
The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that its proximity to a token-vector reflects co-occurrence and conditioned probability.
Attention contributes a potentially redundant association-bias to the encoding walk, which aggregates features from the context via filtering and aggregation operations.
A three-way correspondence between similarity, association, and angular proximity is established in embedding space, leading to an associative organization.
papers.limitation: Experiments on concept space theory were limited to a single benchmark (Hellaswag) and a few models.
future_direction: Further investigation into the relative impact of vector similarity, position biases, filters, and decoding method across various model flavors.
papers.abstract: Transformer based language models exhibit intelligent behaviors such as understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, acquiring knowledge, reasoning, planning, reflecting and using tools. This paper explores how their underlying mechanics give rise to intelligent behaviors. Towards that end, we propose framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space. Examining Transformers through this perspective reveals key insights, establishing a Theory of Transformers: 1) Intelligent behaviours map to paths in Embedding Space which, the Transformer random-walks through during inferencing. 2) LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths. `Intelligence' is learnt by assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors. No learning can take place in-context; context only narrows the subset of paths sampled during decoding. 5) The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that it's proximity to a token-vector reflects its co-occurrence and conditioned probability. Thus, the physical arrangement of vectors in Embedding Space determines path probabilities. 6) Context vectors are composed by aggregating features of the sequence's tokens via a process we call the encoding walk. Attention contributes a - potentially redundant - association-bias to this process. 7) This process is comprised of two principal operation types: filtering (data independent) and aggregation (data dependent). This generalization unifies Transformers with other sequence models. Building upon this foundation, we formalize a popular semantic interpretation of embeddings into a ``concept-space theory'' and find some evidence of it's validity.

papers.title: AgentCoMa: A Compositional Benchmark Mixing Commonsense and Mathematical Reasoning in Real-World Scenarios
papers.research_question: How well do LLMs perform on compositional tasks that require both commonsense and mathematical reasoning, and what is the compositionality gap compared to individual steps and human performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AgentCoMa, a benchmark for mixed-type compositional reasoning, and shows that LLMs exhibit a large compositionality gap (~30% drop) when combining commonsense and math steps, unlike humans.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are brittle in mixed-type compositional reasoning, and AgentCoMa provides a testbed for evaluating and improving such abilities.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show a large compositionality gap (~30% average accuracy drop) when solving tasks requiring both commonsense and math reasoning, despite high accuracy on individual steps.
Human annotators do not show a significant compositionality gap, solving compositional questions and individual steps with similarly high accuracy.
The compositionality gap is substantially larger for mixed-type reasoning than for benchmarks with same-type reasoning steps (e.g., Bamboogle, MultiArith).
Mixed-type reasoning questions are relatively rare in LLM training data, leading models to activate neurons associated with only one reasoning type (math) during composition.
The gap persists across model sizes, families, and tuning strategies (instruction-tuned, SFT, RL), indicating a fundamental brittleness.
papers.limitation:
AgentCoMa is limited to two reasoning types (commonsense and math) and five agentic domains.
Interpretability analysis is limited to a subset of models and may not generalize to all architectures.
future_direction: Extend AgentCoMa to more reasoning types and domains.
Investigate whether fine-tuning on AgentCoMa reduces the compositionality gap.
Explore other interpretability methods to better understand the failure modes.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved high accuracy on complex commonsense and mathematical problems that involve the composition of multiple reasoning steps. However, current compositional benchmarks testing these skills tend to focus on either commonsense or math reasoning, whereas LLM agents solving real-world tasks would require a combination of both. In this work, we introduce an Agentic Commonsense and Math benchmark (AgentCoMa), where each compositional task requires a commonsense reasoning step and a math reasoning step. We test it on 61 LLMs of different sizes, model families, and training strategies. We find that LLMs can usually solve both steps in isolation, yet their accuracy drops by ~30% on average when the two are combined. This is a substantially greater performance gap than the one we observe in prior compositional benchmarks that combine multiple steps of the same reasoning type. In contrast, non-expert human annotators can solve the compositional questions and the individual steps in AgentCoMa with similarly high accuracy. Furthermore, we conduct a series of interpretability studies to better understand the performance gap, examining neuron patterns, attention maps and membership inference. Our work underscores a substantial degree of model brittleness in the context of mixed-type compositional reasoning and offers a test bed for future improvement.

papers.title: On the Binding Problem in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the underlying cause for neural networks' shortcoming in human-level generalization? The paper argues it is the binding problem, the inability to dynamically and flexibly bind distributed information.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a unifying framework for the binding problem in neural networks, organizing it into three aspects: segregation (forming entities from inputs), representation (maintaining separation of information), and composition (using entities for inference).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a compositional approach to AI, based on grounded symbol-like representations, is fundamental for human-level generalization, and hopes this survey serves as a reference and inspiration for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks lack the ability to dynamically bind distributed information, which is crucial for compositional understanding and systematic generalization.
The binding problem can be divided into three functional aspects: segregation, representation, and composition.
Solving the binding problem requires incorporating inductive biases that enable symbolic processing to emerge within connectionist frameworks.
Existing mechanisms like attention, memory, and graph neural networks partially address aspects of the binding problem but a unified solution is still needed.
A unified approach within connectionism is preferable to hybrid neuro-symbolic systems for achieving human-level generalization.
papers.abstract: Contemporary neural networks still fall short of human-level generalization, which extends far beyond our direct experiences. In this paper, we argue that the underlying cause for this shortcoming is their inability to dynamically and flexibly bind information that is distributed throughout the network. This binding problem affects their capacity to acquire a compositional understanding of the world in terms of symbol-like entities (like objects), which is crucial for generalizing in predictable and systematic ways. To address this issue, we propose a unifying framework that revolves around forming meaningful entities from unstructured sensory inputs (segregation), maintaining this separation of information at a representational level (representation), and using these entities to construct new inferences, predictions, and behaviors (composition). Our analysis draws inspiration from a wealth of research in neuroscience and cognitive psychology, and surveys relevant mechanisms from the machine learning literature, to help identify a combination of inductive biases that allow symbolic information processing to emerge naturally in neural networks. We believe that a compositional approach to AI, in terms of grounded symbol-like representations, is of fundamental importance for realizing human-level generalization, and we hope that this paper may contribute towards that goal as a reference and inspiration.

papers.title: Exploring Compositionality in Vision Transformers using Wavelet Representations
papers.research_question: Does the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder exhibit compositionality in its representations? Specifically, can the representation of an image be composed from the representations of its wavelet primitives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to test compositionality in ViT encoder representations using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) primitives and shows that ViT encoder representations are approximately compositional for one-level DWT decomposition.
papers.conclusion: ViT encoder representations exhibit compositional behavior when using primitives from a one-level DWT decomposition, providing a new perspective on how ViTs structure information.
papers.key_findings:
Simple summation of wavelet primitive representations does not reconstruct the original image's representation, indicating a lack of strict compositionality under addition.
A learnable linear composition function can approximate the original image's representation from the wavelet primitive representations, especially for one-level DWT decomposition.
The learned composition function assigns significantly higher weight to the low-pass (approximation) sub-band compared to detail sub-bands.
The proposed compositionality framework is robust to image distortions such as JPEG compression and additive Gaussian noise.
Compositionality is observed in the final encoder layer of ViT models (ViT-B and ViT-L) when using one-level DWT decomposition.
papers.limitation: The analysis is restricted to the final encoder layer of the ViT.
future_direction: Explore all encoder layers of the ViT for potential compositionality.
Explore other ways to study the error in composition.
papers.abstract: While insights into the workings of the transformer model have largely emerged by analysing their behaviour on language tasks, this work investigates the representations learnt by the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder through the lens of compositionality. We introduce a framework, analogous to prior work on measuring compositionality in representation learning, to test for compositionality in the ViT encoder. Crucial to drawing this analogy is the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), which is a simple yet effective tool for obtaining input-dependent primitives in the vision setting. By examining the ability of composed representations to reproduce original image representations, we empirically test the extent to which compositionality is respected in the representation space. Our findings show that primitives from a one-level DWT decomposition produce encoder representations that approximately compose in latent space, offering a new perspective on how ViTs structure information.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Does ChatGPT Have a Mind?
papers.research_question: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLMs have robust internal representations that satisfy various philosophical conditions, but the question of whether they have robust action dispositions for a full folk psychology remains open. It also contends that existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is strong evidence for LLM representation, but the question of whether they have full folk psychological states (beliefs and desires) remains open, particularly due to issues of action dispositions and stability.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs satisfy informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic conditions on mental representation.
LLMs exhibit internal representations that carry information about the world and are causally effective in generating behavior.
LLMs show evidence of world models and structured representations, such as in color and direction concepts.
The behavior of LLMs in game environments suggests they may have action dispositions, but the evidence is not decisive.
Skeptical challenges (sensory grounding, stochastic parrots, memorization) do not undermine the case for LLM representation.
papers.limitation: LLM outputs are very sensitive to prompting, which makes it hard to see the LLM as taking a wide range of means to promote a unified goal.
future_direction: Exploring how stable LLM outputs are to a range of different prompting environments.
Investigating whether LLMs have anything analogous to enduring goals or values.
Further research on how LLM strategies in game environments change under different prompting conditions.
papers.abstract: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions. We approach this question by investigating two key aspects: internal representations and dispositions to act. First, we survey various philosophical theories of representation, including informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic accounts, arguing that LLMs satisfy key conditions proposed by each. We draw on recent interpretability research in machine learning to support these claims. Second, we explore whether LLMs exhibit robust dispositions to perform actions, a necessary component of folk psychology. We consider two prominent philosophical traditions, interpretationism and representationalism, to assess LLM action dispositions. While we find evidence suggesting LLMs may satisfy some criteria for having a mind, particularly in game-theoretic environments, we conclude that the data remains inconclusive. Additionally, we reply to several skeptical challenges to LLM folk psychology, including issues of sensory grounding, the "stochastic parrots" argument, and concerns about memorization. Our paper has three main upshots. First, LLMs do have robust internal representations. Second, there is an open question to answer about whether LLMs have robust action dispositions. Third, existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: From Passive to Persuasive: Steering Emotional Nuance in Human-AI Negotiation
papers.research_question: Whether complex social behaviors, such as empathy and strategic politeness, are encoded as localized, approximately linear directions in LLM activation space and can be effectively steered via attribution-guided activation injection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces STAR, a two-stage inference-time framework that uses attribution patching to localize where behavioral traits causally originate and injects contrastive activation vectors at those positions. It demonstrates that complex interpersonal behaviors are encoded as localized, linear directions in activation space and can be effectively steered.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that complex interpersonal stances are recoverable as precise, localized directions in residual stream space, and that the central challenge in behavioral alignment is identifying where behavioral intent is encoded, not model capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Localized activation injection (STAR) consistently outperforms global steering and instruction priming across emotional dialogue and negotiation tasks.
Steering effects persist and can compound across multi-turn interactions, with larger effect sizes than in single-turn settings.
Human evaluation confirms that automatic metric gains reflect genuine improvements in perceived conversational quality, not superficial lexical changes.
Attribution patching reveals that behavioral traits localize to specific early-layer attention and MLP components, with distinct patterns for affective vs. strategic tasks.
The work challenges the assumption that complex, context-dependent social behaviors resist linear decomposition in activation space.
papers.limitation: Failure modes include verbatim self-repetition, context mismatch, and register over-inflation where affective framing is applied disproportionately.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing conversational fluency, yet instilling them with nuanced, human-like emotional expression remains a significant challenge. Current alignment techniques often address surface-level output or require extensive fine-tuning. This paper demonstrates that targeted activation engineering can steer LLaMA 3.1-8B to exhibit more human-like emotional nuances. We first employ attribution patching to identify causally influential components, to find a key intervention locus by observing activation patterns during diagnostic conversational tasks. We then derive emotional expression vectors from the difference in the activations generated by contrastive text pairs (positive vs. negative examples of target emotions). Applying these vectors to new conversational prompts significantly enhances emotional characteristics: steered responses show increased positive sentiment (e.g., joy, trust) and more frequent first-person pronoun usage, indicative of greater personal engagement. Our findings offer a precise and interpretable framework and new directions for the study of conversational AI.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Representations as Language: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Interpretability
papers.research_question: What systematic structures emerge in the representations learned by transformers, and how do they relate to generalization and training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework for interpretability that quantifies structure in representations, identifies two phases of training, and shows how representational structure relates to generalization and model size.
papers.conclusion: The linguistically-motivated approach helps characterize training dynamics and explain generalization, and suggests that intuitions from linguistics and cognitive science about good representations transfer to deep learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct phases of training: an initial phase of in-distribution learning where representations align with token and part-of-speech information, and a second phase where representations become robust to noise and compress.
Generalization performance improves during the second phase, linking generalization to robustness to noise.
Larger models compress their representations more than smaller models.
The proposed measures (information, variation, regularity, disentanglement) can predict which models will generalize best based on their representational structure.
papers.limitation:
Some results may be particular to the hyperparameters used for training.
The entropy estimation method is an approximation and makes minimal assumptions, but is invariant to linear transformations.
future_direction: Apply the analysis to large-scale translation tasks.
Extend the approach to other levels of abstraction and other models.
papers.abstract: Large scale neural models show impressive performance across a wide array of linguistic tasks. Despite this they remain, largely, black-boxes - inducing vector-representations of their input that prove difficult to interpret. This limits our ability to understand what they learn, and when the learn it, or describe what kinds of representations generalise well out of distribution. To address this we introduce a novel approach to interpretability that looks at the mapping a model learns from sentences to representations as a kind of language in its own right. In doing so we introduce a set of information-theoretic measures that quantify how structured a model's representations are with respect to its input, and when during training that structure arises. Our measures are fast to compute, grounded in linguistic theory, and can predict which models will generalise best based on their representations. We use these measures to describe two distinct phases of training a transformer: an initial phase of in-distribution learning which reduces task loss, then a second stage where representations becoming robust to noise. Generalisation performance begins to increase during this second phase, drawing a link between generalisation and robustness to noise. Finally we look at how model size affects the structure of the representational space, showing that larger models ultimately compress their representations more than their smaller counterparts.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Linguistic generalization and compositionality in modern artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How do modern deep artificial neural networks achieve linguistic generalization and productivity, and do they rely on systematic compositional rules?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews evidence that modern deep neural networks can achieve sophisticated linguistic generalization without relying on systematic compositional rules, and argues this behavior offers a new perspective on computational strategies for linguistic productivity relevant to cognitive science.
papers.conclusion: Modern deep neural networks are proficient at language processing and exhibit subtle grammatical generalization, yet they do not rely on systematic compositional rules, offering a comparative perspective for studying linguistic productivity and non-systematic generalization patterns in human language.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can capture abstract, structure-dependent grammatical generalizations (e.g., long-distance number agreement) even in nonsensical sentences.
These networks fail at systematic compositional generalization in controlled tasks like the SCAN benchmark (e.g., jump and around-right splits).
Some architectures (e.g., convolutional seq2seq) show partial success on compositional splits but without systematicity, making errors uniformly across composition frames.
In communication games, neural networks can develop productive but non-compositional codes that generalize as well as compositional ones.
Analysis of a network's internal circuitry (e.g., ablation studies) suggests it develops genuine grammatical processing mechanisms rather than relying on surface heuristics.
papers.limitation: Our current understanding of the strategies learned by these networks is very limited, and better analytical tools are needed to uncover the mechanisms behind the dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.
future_direction: Develop better analytical tools to uncover the mechanisms that lead to the detected dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.

Investigate whether making neural networks more compositional, for example by means of more structured modular architectures, will make them more adaptive and faster at learning without sacrificing generality.

Use progress in understanding the linguistic capabilities of neural networks to make precise predictions about the origin, scope, and mechanics of non-systematic productive phenomena in human language.
papers.abstract: In the last decade, deep artificial neural networks have achieved astounding performance in many natural language-processing tasks. Given the high productivity of language, these models must possess effective generalization abilities. It is widely assumed that humans handle linguistic productivity by means of algebraic compositional rules: are deep networks similarly compositional? After reviewing the main innovations characterizing current deep language-processing networks, I discuss a set of studies suggesting that deep networks are capable of subtle grammar-dependent generalizations, but also that they do not rely on systematic compositional rules. I argue that the intriguing behaviour of these devices (still awaiting a full understanding) should be of interest to linguists and cognitive scientists, as it offers a new perspective on possible computational strategies to deal with linguistic productivity beyond rule-based compositionality, and it might lead to new insights into the less systematic generalization patterns that also appear in natural language. This article is part of the theme issue 'Towards mechanistic models of meaning composition'.

papers.title: Towards Ethical Multi-Agent Systems of Large Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can we ensure ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of large language models (MALMs) from a mechanistic interpretability perspective? The paper outlines three research challenges: developing evaluation frameworks, explaining failures via mechanistic interpretability, and enabling ethical behavior via targeted interventions.
papers.core_contribution: This position paper outlines a research agenda for ensuring ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of LLMs (MALMs) through mechanistic interpretability, focusing on three interconnected challenges: developing evaluation frameworks, explaining failures via mechanistic interpretability, and enabling ethical behavior via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues for a mechanistic interpretability approach to ensure ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of LLMs, identifying three research directions: evaluation frameworks combining behavioral testing with mechanistic analysis, mechanistic explanation through circuit discovery, and targeted intervention via mechanism-guided parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
Scaling mechanistic analysis to large multi-agent populations remains computationally demanding.
Trade-offs between interpretability and system performance require careful navigation.
Open questions persist about how mechanistic insights generalize across different MALM architectures, task domains, and deployment contexts.
future_direction: Combine mechanistic interpretability with other alignment strategies for MALMs, such as reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF).
Explore complementary approaches to explainability that target higher-level intentions and decisions.
Develop evaluation frameworks that assess ethical behavior at individual, interactional, and systemic levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed in various applications, often functioning as autonomous agents that interact with each other in multi-agent systems. While these systems have shown promise in enhancing capabilities and enabling complex tasks, they also pose significant ethical challenges. This position paper outlines a research agenda aimed at ensuring the ethical behavior of multi-agent systems of LLMs (MALMs) from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability. We identify three key research challenges: (i) developing comprehensive evaluation frameworks to assess ethical behavior at individual, interactional, and systemic levels; (ii) elucidating the internal mechanisms that give rise to emergent behaviors through mechanistic interpretability; and (iii) implementing targeted parameter-efficient alignment techniques to steer MALMs towards ethical behaviors without compromising their performance.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Symbol Processing for In-Context Learning in Transformer Networks
papers.research_question: How can transformer networks perform abstract, semantics-free symbol processing through in-context learning, and can insights from symbolic AI and transformer architecture help design such networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Transformer Production Framework (TPF), which shows how transformer networks can be programmed to perform semantics-free symbol processing through in-context learning, and demonstrates that such transformers are Turing-complete.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform abstract symbol processing through mechanisms akin to production systems, and the TPF offers a path to more interpretable and capable transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can implement production system programs via attention mechanisms, enabling semantics-free symbol processing.
The Discrete-Attention-only Transformer (DAT) can achieve 100% accuracy on the Templatic Generation Task.
The Production System Language (PSL) is Turing-complete, so transformers can be universal computers.
The framework provides a fully interpretable transformer by construction.
The work suggests that transformers' symbol processing abilities may arise from mechanisms similar to induction heads and state-variable encodings.
papers.limitation: The work addresses computability, not learnability, by transformer networks.
future_direction: Combining the new attention heads with traditional attention heads in a new type of transformer.
Testing whether trained language models use similar mechanisms for symbol processing.
Extending compositionality further.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive abilities in symbol processing through in-context learning (ICL). This success flies in the face of decades of critiques asserting that artificial neural networks cannot master abstract symbol manipulation. We seek to understand the mechanisms that can enable robust symbol processing in transformer networks, illuminating both the unanticipated success, and the significant limitations, of transformers in symbol processing. Borrowing insights from symbolic AI and cognitive science on the power of Production System architectures, we develop a high-level Production System Language, PSL, that allows us to write symbolic programs to do complex, abstract symbol processing, and create compilers that precisely implement PSL programs in transformer networks which are, by construction, 100% mechanistically interpretable. The work is driven by study of a purely abstract (semantics-free) symbolic task that we develop, Templatic Generation (TGT). Although developed through study of TGT, PSL is, we demonstrate, highly general: it is Turing Universal. The new type of transformer architecture that we compile from PSL programs suggests a number of paths for enhancing transformers' capabilities at symbol processing. We note, however, that the work we report addresses computability, and not learnability, by transformer networks. Note: The first section provides an extended synopsis of the entire paper.

papers.title: Decomposing Theory of Mind: How Emotional Processing Mediates ToM Abilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: What cognitive processes change in LLMs when activation steering improves Theory of Mind performance, and how does emotional processing mediate these abilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that improved Theory of Mind performance in LLMs via activation steering is mediated by increased emotional processing and decreased analytical processes, suggesting emotional understanding is key to perspective-taking.
papers.conclusion: Steering improves ToM by enhancing emotional and generative processes while inhibiting analytical ones, offering a new mechanistic understanding of perspective-taking in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering improves ToM accuracy on belief attribution tasks by 14.2% (from 32.5% to 46.7%).
Emotional processes (e.g., emotion perception, emotion valuing) are amplified during successful perspective-taking.
Analytical processes (e.g., questioning, convergent thinking) are suppressed during successful perspective-taking.
Cognitive action probes can effectively decompose and analyze steering effects on internal processes.
Successful perspective-taking in LLMs is mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.
papers.limitation: Findings may not generalize to human cognition, and the methodology does not validate such comparisons.
future_direction: Validate findings with multiple, bigger models and additional data sources.
papers.abstract: Recent work shows activation steering substantially improves language models' Theory of Mind (ToM) (Bortoletto et al. 2024), yet the mechanisms of what changes occur internally that leads to different outputs remains unclear. We propose decomposing ToM in LLMs by comparing steered versus baseline LLMs' activations using linear probes trained on 45 cognitive actions. We applied Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering to Gemma-3-4B and evaluated it on 1,000 BigToM forward belief scenarios (Gandhi et al. 2023), we find improved performance on belief attribution tasks (32.5\% to 46.7\% accuracy) is mediated by activations processing emotional content : emotion perception (+2.23), emotion valuing (+2.20), while suppressing analytical processes: questioning (-0.78), convergent thinking (-1.59). This suggests that successful ToM abilities in LLMs are mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: Exploring the Spectrum of Visio-Linguistic Compositionality and Recognition
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between visio-linguistic compositionality and recognition in vision and language models, and what trade-offs exist between these two capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation toolkit for vision-language models, assessing both compositionality and recognition across a wide range of models and benchmarks, revealing trade-offs between these two capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper highlights the necessity of strategies that concurrently enhance both compositionality and recognition in VLMs, and provides an evaluation framework that lays the groundwork for future advancements.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained VLMs show a positive correlation between compositionality and zero-shot classification performance.
Improved pre-training objectives do not always guarantee enhanced compositionality.
Compositionality improves with data scaling, and pre-training with real images is more efficient than synthetic images.
Fine-tuning for compositionality leads to trade-offs, often improving compositionality at the cost of recognition accuracy.
The trade-offs in retrieval tasks depend on the similarity between the fine-tuning data and the evaluation data.
future_direction: Developing training schemes that improve compositionality without sacrificing recognition ability
Creating evaluation tasks independent from training data to avoid knowledge transfer
papers.abstract: Vision and language models (VLMs) such as CLIP have showcased remarkable zero-shot recognition abilities yet face challenges in visio-linguistic compositionality, particularly in linguistic comprehension and fine-grained image-text alignment. This paper explores the intricate relationship between compositionality and recognition -- two pivotal aspects of VLM capability. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of existing VLMs, covering both pre-training approaches aimed at recognition and the fine-tuning methods designed to improve compositionality. Our evaluation employs 12 benchmarks for compositionality, along with 21 zero-shot classification and two retrieval benchmarks for recognition. In our analysis from 274 CLIP model checkpoints, we reveal patterns and trade-offs that emerge between compositional understanding and recognition accuracy. Ultimately, this necessitates strategic efforts towards developing models that improve both capabilities, as well as the meticulous formulation of benchmarks for compositionality. We open our evaluation framework at https://github.com/ytaek-oh/vl_compo.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Sectoral Coupling in Linguistic State Space
papers.research_question: How can inter-functional dependencies between cognitive subsystems (Semantic Sectors) within an artificial agent's belief state be formally quantified?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a formal framework of intra-level sectoral coupling constants (gk_ij) to quantify the influence between functional Semantic Sectors within an abstraction level, forming a coupling profile G that determines an agent's cognitive style and dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a quantitative, mechanistic, and interpretable model of agent cognition, enabling the analysis of internal dynamics and contributing to the development of safer, more predictable, and governable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
The framework defines intra-level sectoral coupling constants gk_ij that quantify the influence pathway from a source Semantic Sector to a target Semantic Sector within a specific abstraction level.
The complete coupling profile G = {gk_ij} serves as a quantitative signature of an agent's internal processing architecture, shaping its cognitive dynamics and behavioral style.
Distinct coupling profiles give rise to emergent cognitive styles (e.g., 'reactive' vs. 'deliberative') and dynamics like feedback loops.
Methodologies for measuring and inferring gk_ij values from agent data (internal logs or observable behavior) are outlined.
The coupling profile is dynamic and can evolve across abstraction levels via 'coupling propagation' and is subject to perturbations that alter cognitive processing.
papers.limitation:
Overall model complexity and parameter explosion due to the potentially vast matrix of intra-level coupling constants across many sectors and abstraction levels.
Measurement fidelity and identifiability challenges in reliably inferring gk_ij values from observable data due to partial observability and interacting parameters.
Scalability challenges in simulating agents with extensive belief states and dense coupling matrices.
Challenges in developing robust and data-efficient machine learning algorithms to learn the coupling profile G and operator parameters.
future_direction: Developing a 'G-Map'—a neural network that learns the transformation from an agent's foundational neural network weights to its emergent coupling profile G, enabling 'meta-tuning'.
Exploring the concept of 'gauge equivalence' in agent architectures, where different weight configurations result in the same functional coupling profile.
Pursuing experimental strategies for G-Map development, including dataset generation, model training, and validation.
papers.abstract: This work presents a formal framework for quantifying the internal dependencies between functional subsystems within artificial agents whose belief states are composed of structured linguistic fragments. Building on the Semantic Manifold framework, which organizes belief content into functional sectors and stratifies them across hierarchical levels of abstraction, we introduce a system of sectoral coupling constants that characterize how one cognitive sector influences another within a fixed level of abstraction. The complete set of these constants forms an agent-specific coupling profile that governs internal information flow, shaping the agent's overall processing tendencies and cognitive style.
