papers.conclusion: The paper argues for a mechanistic interpretability approach to ensure ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of LLMs, identifying three research directions: evaluation frameworks combining behavioral testing with mechanistic analysis, mechanistic explanation through circuit discovery, and targeted intervention via mechanism-guided parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
Scaling mechanistic analysis to large multi-agent populations remains computationally demanding.
Trade-offs between interpretability and system performance require careful navigation.
Open questions persist about how mechanistic insights generalize across different MALM architectures, task domains, and deployment contexts.
future_direction: Combine mechanistic interpretability with other alignment strategies for MALMs, such as reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF).
Explore complementary approaches to explainability that target higher-level intentions and decisions.
Develop evaluation frameworks that assess ethical behavior at individual, interactional, and systemic levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed in various applications, often functioning as autonomous agents that interact with each other in multi-agent systems. While these systems have shown promise in enhancing capabilities and enabling complex tasks, they also pose significant ethical challenges. This position paper outlines a research agenda aimed at ensuring the ethical behavior of multi-agent systems of LLMs (MALMs) from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability. We identify three key research challenges: (i) developing comprehensive evaluation frameworks to assess ethical behavior at individual, interactional, and systemic levels; (ii) elucidating the internal mechanisms that give rise to emergent behaviors through mechanistic interpretability; and (iii) implementing targeted parameter-efficient alignment techniques to steer MALMs towards ethical behaviors without compromising their performance.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Symbol Processing for In-Context Learning in Transformer Networks
papers.research_question: How can transformer networks perform abstract, semantics-free symbol processing through in-context learning, and can insights from symbolic AI and transformer architecture help design such networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Transformer Production Framework (TPF), which shows how transformer networks can be programmed to perform semantics-free symbol processing through in-context learning, and demonstrates that such transformers are Turing-complete.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform abstract symbol processing through mechanisms akin to production systems, and the TPF offers a path to more interpretable and capable transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can implement production system programs via attention mechanisms, enabling semantics-free symbol processing.
The Discrete-Attention-only Transformer (DAT) can achieve 100% accuracy on the Templatic Generation Task.
The Production System Language (PSL) is Turing-complete, so transformers can be universal computers.
The framework provides a fully interpretable transformer by construction.
The work suggests that transformers' symbol processing abilities may arise from mechanisms similar to induction heads and state-variable encodings.
papers.limitation: The work addresses computability, not learnability, by transformer networks.
future_direction: Combining the new attention heads with traditional attention heads in a new type of transformer.
Testing whether trained language models use similar mechanisms for symbol processing.
Extending compositionality further.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive abilities in symbol processing through in-context learning (ICL). This success flies in the face of decades of critiques asserting that artificial neural networks cannot master abstract symbol manipulation. We seek to understand the mechanisms that can enable robust symbol processing in transformer networks, illuminating both the unanticipated success, and the significant limitations, of transformers in symbol processing. Borrowing insights from symbolic AI and cognitive science on the power of Production System architectures, we develop a high-level Production System Language, PSL, that allows us to write symbolic programs to do complex, abstract symbol processing, and create compilers that precisely implement PSL programs in transformer networks which are, by construction, 100% mechanistically interpretable. The work is driven by study of a purely abstract (semantics-free) symbolic task that we develop, Templatic Generation (TGT). Although developed through study of TGT, PSL is, we demonstrate, highly general: it is Turing Universal. The new type of transformer architecture that we compile from PSL programs suggests a number of paths for enhancing transformers' capabilities at symbol processing. We note, however, that the work we report addresses computability, and not learnability, by transformer networks. Note: The first section provides an extended synopsis of the entire paper.

papers.title: Decomposing Theory of Mind: How Emotional Processing Mediates ToM Abilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: What cognitive processes change in LLMs when activation steering improves Theory of Mind performance, and how does emotional processing mediate these abilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that improved Theory of Mind performance in LLMs via activation steering is mediated by increased emotional processing and decreased analytical processes, suggesting emotional understanding is key to perspective-taking.
papers.conclusion: Steering improves ToM by enhancing emotional and generative processes while inhibiting analytical ones, offering a new mechanistic understanding of perspective-taking in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering improves ToM accuracy on belief attribution tasks by 14.2% (from 32.5% to 46.7%).
Emotional processes (e.g., emotion perception, emotion valuing) are amplified during successful perspective-taking.
Analytical processes (e.g., questioning, convergent thinking) are suppressed during successful perspective-taking.
Cognitive action probes can effectively decompose and analyze steering effects on internal processes.
Successful perspective-taking in LLMs is mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.
papers.limitation: Findings may not generalize to human cognition, and the methodology does not validate such comparisons.
future_direction: Validate findings with multiple, bigger models and additional data sources.
papers.abstract: Recent work shows activation steering substantially improves language models' Theory of Mind (ToM) (Bortoletto et al. 2024), yet the mechanisms of what changes occur internally that leads to different outputs remains unclear. We propose decomposing ToM in LLMs by comparing steered versus baseline LLMs' activations using linear probes trained on 45 cognitive actions. We applied Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering to Gemma-3-4B and evaluated it on 1,000 BigToM forward belief scenarios (Gandhi et al. 2023), we find improved performance on belief attribution tasks (32.5\% to 46.7\% accuracy) is mediated by activations processing emotional content : emotion perception (+2.23), emotion valuing (+2.20), while suppressing analytical processes: questioning (-0.78), convergent thinking (-1.59). This suggests that successful ToM abilities in LLMs are mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: Exploring the Spectrum of Visio-Linguistic Compositionality and Recognition
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between visio-linguistic compositionality and recognition in vision and language models, and what trade-offs exist between these two capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation toolkit for vision-language models, assessing both compositionality and recognition across a wide range of models and benchmarks, revealing trade-offs between these two capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper highlights the necessity of strategies that concurrently enhance both compositionality and recognition in VLMs, and provides an evaluation framework that lays the groundwork for future advancements.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained VLMs show a positive correlation between compositionality and zero-shot classification performance.
Improved pre-training objectives do not always guarantee enhanced compositionality.
Compositionality improves with data scaling, and pre-training with real images is more efficient than synthetic images.
Fine-tuning for compositionality leads to trade-offs, often improving compositionality at the cost of recognition accuracy.
The trade-offs in retrieval tasks depend on the similarity between the fine-tuning data and the evaluation data.
future_direction: Developing training schemes that improve compositionality without sacrificing recognition ability
Creating evaluation tasks independent from training data to avoid knowledge transfer
papers.abstract: Vision and language models (VLMs) such as CLIP have showcased remarkable zero-shot recognition abilities yet face challenges in visio-linguistic compositionality, particularly in linguistic comprehension and fine-grained image-text alignment. This paper explores the intricate relationship between compositionality and recognition -- two pivotal aspects of VLM capability. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of existing VLMs, covering both pre-training approaches aimed at recognition and the fine-tuning methods designed to improve compositionality. Our evaluation employs 12 benchmarks for compositionality, along with 21 zero-shot classification and two retrieval benchmarks for recognition. In our analysis from 274 CLIP model checkpoints, we reveal patterns and trade-offs that emerge between compositional understanding and recognition accuracy. Ultimately, this necessitates strategic efforts towards developing models that improve both capabilities, as well as the meticulous formulation of benchmarks for compositionality. We open our evaluation framework at https://github.com/ytaek-oh/vl_compo.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Sectoral Coupling in Linguistic State Space
papers.research_question: How can inter-functional dependencies between cognitive subsystems (Semantic Sectors) within an artificial agent's belief state be formally quantified?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a formal framework of intra-level sectoral coupling constants (gk_ij) to quantify the influence between functional Semantic Sectors within an abstraction level, forming a coupling profile G that determines an agent's cognitive style and dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a quantitative, mechanistic, and interpretable model of agent cognition, enabling the analysis of internal dynamics and contributing to the development of safer, more predictable, and governable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
The framework defines intra-level sectoral coupling constants gk_ij that quantify the influence pathway from a source Semantic Sector to a target Semantic Sector within a specific abstraction level.
The complete coupling profile G = {gk_ij} serves as a quantitative signature of an agent's internal processing architecture, shaping its cognitive dynamics and behavioral style.
Distinct coupling profiles give rise to emergent cognitive styles (e.g., 'reactive' vs. 'deliberative') and dynamics like feedback loops.
Methodologies for measuring and inferring gk_ij values from agent data (internal logs or observable behavior) are outlined.
The coupling profile is dynamic and can evolve across abstraction levels via 'coupling propagation' and is subject to perturbations that alter cognitive processing.
papers.limitation:
Overall model complexity and parameter explosion due to the potentially vast matrix of intra-level coupling constants across many sectors and abstraction levels.
Measurement fidelity and identifiability challenges in reliably inferring gk_ij values from observable data due to partial observability and interacting parameters.
Scalability challenges in simulating agents with extensive belief states and dense coupling matrices.
Challenges in developing robust and data-efficient machine learning algorithms to learn the coupling profile G and operator parameters.
future_direction: Developing a 'G-Map'—a neural network that learns the transformation from an agent's foundational neural network weights to its emergent coupling profile G, enabling 'meta-tuning'.
Exploring the concept of 'gauge equivalence' in agent architectures, where different weight configurations result in the same functional coupling profile.
Pursuing experimental strategies for G-Map development, including dataset generation, model training, and validation.
papers.abstract: This work presents a formal framework for quantifying the internal dependencies between functional subsystems within artificial agents whose belief states are composed of structured linguistic fragments. Building on the Semantic Manifold framework, which organizes belief content into functional sectors and stratifies them across hierarchical levels of abstraction, we introduce a system of sectoral coupling constants that characterize how one cognitive sector influences another within a fixed level of abstraction. The complete set of these constants forms an agent-specific coupling profile that governs internal information flow, shaping the agent's overall processing tendencies and cognitive style. We provide a detailed taxonomy of these intra-level coupling roles, covering domains such as perceptual integration, memory access and formation, planning, meta-cognition, execution control, and affective modulation. We also explore how these coupling profiles generate feedback loops, systemic dynamics, and emergent signatures of cognitive behavior. Methodologies for inferring these profiles from behavioral or internal agent data are outlined, along with a discussion of how these couplings evolve across abstraction levels. This framework contributes a mechanistic and interpretable approach to modeling complex cognition, with applications in AI system design, alignment diagnostics, and the analysis of emergent agent behavior.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: Revealing emergent human-like conceptual representations from language prediction
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) develop human-like concepts through language prediction, and how such concepts are represented, organized, and linked to behavior.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge in LLMs purely from language prediction, without real-world grounding. These representations converge to a shared, context-independent structure that predicts model performance and aligns with human behavioral and neural data.
papers.conclusion: The findings establish that critical aspects of human conceptual representation and organization can emerge purely from language prediction in LLMs, offering a tractable window into human concepts and advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from definitional descriptions using in-context learning, with performance improving with more demonstrations.
The conceptual representations formed by LLMs converge toward a shared, context-independent relational structure as the number of contextual demonstrations increases.
Alignment of a model's conceptual representations with this convergent structure reliably predicts its performance on a range of language understanding and reasoning tasks.
LLM-derived conceptual representations effectively predict human behavioral judgments, such as similarity ratings and categorization, outperforming static word embeddings.
The convergent conceptual representations align closely with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for their biological plausibility.
papers.limitation: LLMs struggled to predict human judgments when they relied on perceptual properties like color or texture, indicating a divergence from human judgments in visually grounded dimensions.
papers.abstract: People acquire concepts through rich physical and social experiences and use them to understand and navigate the world. In contrast, large language models (LLMs), trained solely through next-token prediction on text, exhibit strikingly human-like behaviors. Are these models developing concepts akin to those of humans? If so, how are such concepts represented, organized, and related to behavior? Here, we address these questions by investigating the representations formed by LLMs during an in-context concept inference task. We found that LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from linguistic descriptions in relation to contextual cues about other concepts. The derived representations converge toward a shared, context-independent structure, and alignment with this structure reliably predicts model performance across various understanding and reasoning tasks. Moreover, the convergent representations effectively capture human behavioral judgments and closely align with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for biological plausibility. Together, these findings establish that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge purely from language prediction without real-world grounding, highlighting the role of conceptual structure in understanding intelligent behavior. More broadly, our work suggests that LLMs offer a tangible window into the nature of human concepts and lays the groundwork for advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: PragWorld: A Benchmark Evaluating LLMs' Local World Model under Minimal Linguistic Alterations and Conversational Dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models construct an implicit world model of the environment described in the input, and how malleable are these representations under minimal linguistic alterations in conversational contexts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the PRAGWORLD benchmark to evaluate the malleability of LLMs' internal world models under minimal linguistic alterations in conversations, and proposes a dual-perspective interpretability framework to identify harmful/useful layers and improve robustness via layer-regularization fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs have fragile world models that are not robustly accurate under linguistic alterations, but the proposed interpretability framework and regularization techniques can help understand and mitigate these issues.
papers.key_findings:
Language models struggle to maintain robust accuracy under minimal linguistic alterations in conversations, indicating brittleness in their latent world models.
The proposed dual-perspective interpretability framework (using Direct Effect Patching and MLP Zero-Out ablation) can identify transformer layers that encode useful or harmful reasoning patterns.
Fine-tuning models on synthetic data with the proposed regularization techniques (Useful Layer Amplification and Harmful Layer Suppression) improves robust accuracy, especially for smaller models.
Models exhibit a strong bias towards answering 'Yes' or 'No', which is more pronounced in smaller models and persists even after fine-tuning.
Entity tracking ability, i.e., memorizing and updating information about entities in a conversation, improves with model scale and is enhanced by fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Real-world conversations are rich with pragmatic elements, such as entity mentions, references, and implicatures. Understanding such nuances is a requirement for successful natural communication, and often requires building a local world model which encodes such elements and captures the dynamics of their evolving states. However, it is not well-understood whether language models (LMs) construct or maintain a robust implicit representation of conversations. In this work, we evaluate the ability of LMs to encode and update their internal world model in dyadic conversations and test their malleability under linguistic alterations. To facilitate this, we apply seven minimal linguistic alterations to conversations sourced from popular datasets and construct two benchmarks comprising yes-no questions. We evaluate a wide range of open and closed source LMs and observe that they struggle to maintain robust accuracy. Our analysis unveils that LMs struggle to memorize crucial details, such as tracking entities under linguistic alterations to conversations. We then propose a dual-perspective interpretability framework which identifies transformer layers that are useful or harmful and highlights linguistic alterations most influenced by harmful layers, typically due to encoding spurious signals or relying on shortcuts. Inspired by these insights, we propose two layer-regularization based fine-tuning strategies that suppress the effect of the harmful layers.

papers.title: Desiderata for Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can representation learning desiderata (non-spuriousness, efficiency, disentanglement) be formalized using causal notions, and how can metrics and algorithms be developed to learn such representations from single observational datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal framework for representation learning that formalizes desiderata like non-spuriousness, efficiency, and disentanglement using counterfactual notions (probabilities of causation) and provides metrics and algorithms (CAUSAL-REP and IOSS) to learn such representations from single observational datasets.
papers.conclusion: Causality provides a fruitful perspective for representation learning, allowing intuitive desiderata to be formalized and leading to metrics and algorithms that can learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spuriousness and efficiency in supervised representation learning can be formalized using probabilities of sufficiency (PS) and necessity (PN), leading to the CAUSAL-REP algorithm.
Disentanglement in unsupervised representation learning can be formalized via causal disentanglement, leading to the Independence-of-Support Score (IOSS) metric.
CAUSAL-REP learns non-spurious representations that improve out-of-distribution prediction on image and text datasets compared to baseline methods.
IOSS can distinguish disentangled from entangled representations better than existing unsupervised metrics on synthetic and real datasets.
The causal perspective enables the development of calculable metrics and algorithms for representation learning desiderata without requiring multiple environments or labeled features.
papers.limitation:
CAUSAL-REP requires the pinpointability condition (i.e., the unobserved common cause C can be pinpointed from X) for identification.
IOSS assumes compact support of the representation and may not apply to representations with unbounded support.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing non-spuriousness and efficiency (in supervised representation learning) and disentanglement (in unsupervised representation learning) using counterfactual quantities and observable consequences of causal assertions. This yields computable metrics that can be used to assess the degree to which representations satisfy the desiderata of interest and learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Break It Down: Evidence for Structural Compositionality in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks implement compositional solutions by decomposing tasks into modular subnetworks, or do they learn non-compositional templates?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks often implement compositional tasks via modular subnetworks, suggesting they can learn compositionality without symbolic mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit structural compositionality, indicating they can learn compositional representations internally.
papers.key_findings:
Many models implement subroutines in modular subnetworks, which can be ablated while maintaining other functionalities.
Pretraining leads to more consistently compositional structure in language models.
Evidence of structural compositionality varies across tasks and architectures, with some showing strong modularity and others more diffuse implementations.
Control experiments with randomly initialized models show that the discovered subnetworks are not epiphenomenal artifacts.
papers.abstract: Though modern neural networks have achieved impressive performance in both vision and language tasks, we know little about the functions that they implement. One possibility is that neural networks implicitly break down complex tasks into subroutines, implement modular solutions to these subroutines, and compose them into an overall solution to a task - a property we term structural compositionality. Another possibility is that they may simply learn to match new inputs to learned templates, eliding task decomposition entirely. Here, we leverage model pruning techniques to investigate this question in both vision and language across a variety of architectures, tasks, and pretraining regimens. Our results demonstrate that models often implement solutions to subroutines via modular subnetworks, which can be ablated while maintaining the functionality of other subnetworks. This suggests that neural networks may be able to learn compositionality, obviating the need for specialized symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Seeking Neural Nuggets: Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models from a Parametric Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether implicit knowledge stored in the parameters of a larger language model (teacher) can be transferred to a smaller model (student) through a parametric perspective.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parametric knowledge transfer paradigm that extracts task-specific parameters from a teacher model using sensitivity-based techniques and injects them into a student model via LoRA, demonstrating the transferability of implicit knowledge across LLMs of different scales.
papers.conclusion: Parametric knowledge transfer is feasible and effective; the proposed framework successfully transfers knowledge from larger to smaller LLMs, and the analysis highlights key factors that contribute to successful transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Transferring extracted parameters from a teacher to a student model consistently improves the student's performance across reasoning, professional knowledge, instruction-driven, and open-ended conversation benchmarks.
The structural integrity of the extracted parameters (e.g., preserving submatrices) is crucial for effective transfer, outperforming random or single-weight extraction.
Sensitivity-based parameter extraction outperforms random selection, and the origin of parameters (which modules) matters more than the sheer number of parameters transferred.
Scaling up the teacher model generally leads to better student performance, even when there are architectural differences between models.
The number of seed samples used for sensitivity calculation and the initialization strategy for the LoRA module are important factors influencing transfer efficacy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently encode a wealth of knowledge within their parameters through pre-training on extensive corpora. While prior research has delved into operations on these parameters to manipulate the underlying implicit knowledge (encompassing detection, editing, and merging), there remains an ambiguous understanding regarding their transferability across models with varying scales. In this paper, we seek to empirically investigate knowledge transfer from larger to smaller models through a parametric perspective. To achieve this, we employ sensitivity-based techniques to extract and align knowledge-specific parameters between different LLMs. Moreover, the LoRA module is used as the intermediary mechanism for injecting the extracted knowledge into smaller models. Evaluations across four benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposed method. Our findings highlight the critical factors contributing to the process of parametric knowledge transfer, underscoring the transferability of model parameters across LLMs of different scales. Project website: https://maszhongming.github.io/ParaKnowTransfer.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Distributed Specialization: Rare-Token Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do LLMs develop internal specialization mechanisms for rare token processing, and if so, are they modular or distributed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs process rare tokens through distributed specialization: functionally coordinated but spatially distributed subnetworks, rather than discrete modular architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement distributed specialization for rare token processing through parameter-level differentiation within shared architectures, not through discrete modular architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Rare token processing exhibits a three-regime hierarchical influence structure (plateau, power-law, rapid decay) absent for common tokens.
Rare-token neurons exhibit coordinated activation patterns (lower effective dimensionality) despite being spatially distributed.
Rare-token neurons are spatially distributed and do not form clustered modules.
Rare tokens access specialized mechanisms through standard attention pathways without dedicated routing circuits.
Rare-token neurons develop distinct heavy-tailed spectral signatures in their weight correlation matrices.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focuses exclusively on neurons in the last MLP layer, while rare-token processing may involve interactions across multiple layers and attention mechanisms.
The practical impact of identified rare-token neurons on downstream applications remains untested.
future_direction: Extending analysis to earlier MLP layers, attention heads, and residual streams.
Testing the applicability and impact of rare-token neurons on downstream tasks.
Investigating the relationship between rare token specialization and other forms of functional organization in transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with representing and generating rare tokens despite their importance in specialized domains. We investigate whether LLMs develop internal specialization mechanisms through discrete modular architectures or distributed parameter-level differentiation. Through systematic analysis of final-layer MLP neurons across multiple model families, we discover that rare-token processing emerges via \textit{distributed specialization}: functionally coordinated but spatially distributed subnetworks that exhibit three distinct organizational principles. First, we identify a reproducible three-regime influence hierarchy comprising highly influential plateau neurons(also termed as rare-token neurons), power-law decay neurons, and minimally contributing neurons, which is absent in common-token processing. Second, plateau neurons demonstrate coordinated activation patterns (reduced effective dimensionality) while remaining spatially distributed rather than forming discrete clusters. Third, these specialized mechanisms are universally accessible through standard attention pathways without requiring dedicated routing circuits. Training dynamics reveal that functional specialization emerges gradually through parameter differentiation, with specialized neurons developing increasingly heavy-tailed weight correlation spectra consistent with Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization signatures. Our findings establish that LLMs process rare-tokens through distributed coordination within shared architectures rather than mixture-of-experts-style modularity. These results provide insights for interpretable model editing, computational efficiency optimization, and understanding emergent functional organization in transformer networks.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Exploring and Exploiting the Inherent Efficiency within Large Reasoning Models for Self-Guided Efficiency Enhancement
papers.research_question: Can the inherent efficiency within large reasoning models be exploited to reduce overthinking and enhance reasoning efficiency without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that large reasoning models inherently possess untapped efficiency potential, and proposes two self-guided methods—Efficiency Steering (a training-free activation steering technique) and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL (a reinforcement learning framework)—that significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance.
papers.conclusion: Overthinking in large reasoning models is a controllable behavior embedded in internal representations; the proposed self-guided methods (Efficiency Steering and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL) successfully enhance reasoning efficiency without external supervision, offering practical directions for building more cost-efficient reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LRMs exhibit inherent efficiency: the shortest correct reasoning paths are often less than half the length of the longest correct ones, indicating substantial untapped efficiency potential.
Efficient and verbose reasoning paths are linearly separable in the model's representation space, with consistent positional shifts across layers and difficulty levels.
Efficiency Steering, a training-free method that injects a single vector direction derived from contrastive reasoning pairs, can controllably modulate reasoning length without compromising accuracy.
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, which uses a dynamic reward function balancing correctness and brevity, significantly reduces reasoning length while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on simpler mathematical problems (Levels 1-3) leads to efficient reasoning that transfers well to harder problems, suggesting that efficiency priors learned from simple data are effective.
papers.limitation:
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL is sensitive to optimization steps; beyond 30 steps, efficiency improves but correctness can deteriorate, indicating a trade-off that requires careful tuning.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on harder mathematical examples (Levels 4-5) does not yield as favorable efficiency outcomes as training on simpler examples, suggesting that data distribution impacts the method's effectiveness.
future_direction: Further exploration of representational properties of LLMs to build efficiency-aware alignment strategies with minimal external supervision.
Investigating curriculum-aware or simplicity-biased training strategies for self-rewarded efficiency optimization, as simpler problems may provide better efficiency outcomes at lower training cost.
Refining the capabilities that already exist within LRMs for building more efficient and accessible reasoning systems.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced language models' capabilities in complex problem-solving by emulating human-like deliberative thinking. However, these models often exhibit overthinking (i.e., the generation of unnecessarily verbose and redundant content), which hinders efficiency and inflates inference cost. In this work, we explore the representational and behavioral origins of this inefficiency, revealing that LRMs inherently possess the capacity for more concise reasoning. Empirical analyses show that correct reasoning paths vary significantly in length, and the shortest correct responses often suffice, indicating untapped efficiency potential. Exploiting these findings, we propose two lightweight methods to enhance LRM efficiency. First, we introduce Efficiency Steering, a training-free activation steering technique that modulates reasoning behavior via a single direction in the model's representation space. Second, we develop Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically balances task accuracy and brevity by rewarding concise correct solutions. Extensive experiments on seven LRM backbones across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our methods significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance. Our results highlight that reasoning efficiency can be improved by leveraging and guiding the intrinsic capabilities of existing models in a self-guided manner.

papers.title: Developmentally plausible multimodal language models are highly modular
papers.research_question: Do developmentally plausible multimodal language models exhibit modularity, and how does the addition of visual inputs affect the internal processing mechanisms for language tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Developmentally plausible multimodal language models are highly modular, and the presence of visual inputs changes which internal components in the text decoder are used to process the same textual inputs.
papers.conclusion: Developmentally plausible multimodal language models exhibit a high degree of modularity, and adding visual inputs changes how the text decoder processes a task, increasing the amount of shared components between tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The trained GIT models achieve performance similar to the best-performing architectures from the previous BabyLM Challenge.
Visual information does not improve performance on text-only tasks compared to text-only models.
The models exhibit high modularity, with distinct neural components arising to process related tasks.
For text-and-image tasks, adding or removing visual inputs causes the model to use distinct sets of neurons to process the same textual input.
Modal and task-specific specialization is efficiently learned even in small-scale models trained on developmentally plausible data.
papers.limitation: The models are not directly comparable to human learners due to differing inductive biases and a relatively small quantity of visual inputs.
future_direction: Future research could explore the relationship between neuron overlap and task performance across diverse architectures.
Investigating the types and extents of modularity in neural language models to assess parameter efficiency.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate emergent modularity, where functionally specialized components and circuits arise to handle specific tasks or task formats. If similar modules arise in models trained on more cognitively plausible datasets, it could inform debates surrounding what kinds of would be learnable given more human-like language learning signals. In this paper, we describe a multimodal vision-language model submitted to the BabyLM Challenge. Our model achieves similar performance to the best-performing architectures from last year, though visual information does not improve performance on text-only tasks over text-only models (in accordance with prior findings). To better understand how the model processes the evaluation tasks of the BabyLM Challenge, we leverage causal interpretability methods to locate the neurons that contribute to the model`s final decisions. We find that the models we train are highly modular: distinct components arise to process related tasks. Furthermore, on text-and-image tasks, adding or removing visual inputs causes the model to use distinct components to process the same textual inputs. This suggests that modal and task-specific specialization is efficiently learned, and that a high degree of functional specialization arises in even small-scale language models.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Model Organisms for Human Associative Learning
